comments.author: SwellJoe
comments.text: Dang, the prices are crazy. $10k for the lowest tier? I expect federal data to be free. Most federal data related to stuff like regulation (e.g. FCC spectrum use coverage maps), maps for federally-managed lands, etc. is free. And, it should be free. It's a core part of accountability and transparency. Historically there was a copying cost (having a human print physical copies on paper or CD/DVD/tape), which is understandable, but now that the incremental cost of each new copy approaches $0, that's what it should cost users of the data.

comments.author: xp84
comments.text:
This is interesting. For a long time it was pointed out that ZIP codes, unlike say, city or state boundaries, were not properly representable as polygons, since they don't divide up acreage into zones, but rather label postal delivery routes. Suppose I build a new neighborhood way out in the middle of nowhere. The "polygon" concept suggests that we could look and see what polygon I'm in, and that will determine what post office delivers my mail. But in reality, if there was no route to that area already, they could decide to make it part of any one of the surrounding routes.
I suppose though, as long as you let the polygons map has uncontained areas, where no routes currently exist, it's a doable task to draw polygons around the limits of every route network, as long as you don't mind that they may have lots of weird ragged edges.

comments.author: jlhawn
comments.text:
I wonder if this could be used anywhere as an alternative to Lloyd's algorithm. I have a hobby project which uses Lloyd's to "relax" an icosohedral equal area mesh on the surface of a sphere [1]. I'm going to try to swap it out with an adaptation of this and see if it's much better or if I can afford more iterations with this method.
Edit: tried it, and it’s definitely
not
better for this use case. e-means wins by needing fewer passes over a huge dataset, but relaxing a mesh on a sphere has no dataset: each Voronoi cell’s centroid can be computed directly from its geometry. Mini-batches just swap that for a noisy sampled estimate of the same thing. It has the same objective and the same optimum, so at best it matches Lloyd. In practice it was much slower and left the grid noisy, and with small sample budgets it even tangled the mesh.
[1]

One summer, I had brought a book on how to make different paper airplanes.  My grandmother had this huge crate of dot matrix printer paper [1] that I was given freedom to use to my heart's content.
I made hundreds of planes, of varying quality.  I even did quasi-scientific tests to see which ones would fly farther, and I used a rubber band extended to the same length each time to try and ensure I was applying roughly the same amount of force in each launch.
I look back at that time pretty fondly.  It was the only time in my life that I actually had fun visiting my grandmother's house.

That's also a fairly pared down version of the Chrome engine, designed for embedding used by tons of projects, like games for their in game lobbies or OBS for their Web overlays.
Personally, my problem with CEF is that it keeps Chrome fairly vanilla - and there's a

Zebkit on the other hand sounds like it's gonna be more granular - we'll if they cope with this better, but I think there's definitely a market for a much more lightweight browser engine that's broadly compatible - for example, just getting rid of sandboxes and process isolation would be a huge but incompatbile change.

A note to anyone going down this road, just as an aside: actually shipping w/ Chromium ( and especially w/ FFmpeg ) can get complicated.
